title: When words run out
job: Paraphrase, ask what something means, repair a misunderstanding
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: lam afham + , + hal yumkinuka an tuʿīd

rules.text: REPAIR IS THREE FRAMES AND TWO VERBS. shayʾ mithl and nawʿ min describe around a gap; bi-ʿibāra ukhrā restates your own words; L5-M5's mā maʿnā asks about someone else's. Every pragmatic move here you have already made in some language.

English repairs by APOLOGISING FIRST — sorry, I didn't catch that. An Arabic repair that opens with āsif every time reads as distress rather than as politeness. The direct question is the polite form here.
English or HEDGES inside a paraphrase: a chair, or something. Arabic aw is a real disjunction and means one or the other. The hedging is done by mithl and nawʿ min, and aw softens nothing.

TWO VERBS THE LADDER NEVER BOUGHT until this rung. afham is to understand what was said; aʿrif is to know. Thirty-nine modules ran with neither, so these notes are written for the whole course and not for this module.
aʿrif is knowing a THING — a word, a street, a face. aʿlam is knowing THAT something is so, and anna follows it. English lets one verb do both and Arabic does not, so the choice is forced every time.

Bare mā does three jobs and this is where the course pays for it: what in a question, that which as a free relative, and the older negator you meet in a saying. L5-M1's proverbs index whole precisely so that this row could exist.
yusammā and tusammā, is called, are L4-M7's internal passive doing an ordinary conversational job. The official register you met at a counter is the same grammar you now need at a table.

This is NOT the indirect request. Asking what a word means is direct, and that is the point: M7's veiling would make a repair harder to answer rather than easier, and an apology (M4) would make it heavier.

kalima and kalimāt are L5-M3's, maʿnā and shayʾ are L5-M5's, mithl is L5-M1's. The new keys here are the PHRASES built on them — shayʾ mithl, nawʿ min, bi-ʿibāra ukhrā, kayfa taqūl — not the words inside.

words.note: Three jobs in one word: what in a question about a thing, that which as a relative, and an older not in a saying. Which one it is comes from the sentence around it.
L1-M9's ʿarabiyya with bi- on the front: in the language, not from it. Said bil-ʿarabiyya, the article swallowed.

sentences.trap: mā asks about a THING and man asks about a person; English what covers both when it should not. Pointing at someone and saying mā hādhā is a real rudeness, not a grammar slip.
sentences.sound: MĀ is one long beat. bi-al-ʿa-ra-BIY-ya collapses to bil-, and the ʿayn is squeezed shut before the ra.

variations.cue: What is this in Arabic?
variations.changed: the pointing word, agreeing with a feminine thing

variations.cue: How do you say this in Arabic?
variations.changed: asking for the word rather than about the thing

mistake.why: fī is inside a place. A language takes bi-, so it is bi-al-ʿarabiyya — and the same bi- gives bi-al-inklīziyya for the other direction.

sentences.usage: Pointing at an object you cannot name. The most useful sentence in the level and the least embarrassing to say.

sentences.display: mā maʿnā hādhihi al-kalima. lam afham
sentences.script: ما معنى هذه الكلمة. لم أفهم
sentences.cue: What does this word mean? I did not understand.
sentences.literal: what meaning-of this the-word. not I-understood

words.note: To understand what was said. lam afham, with L3-M4's lam, is the past: I did not follow. fahimtu is the plain past, I understood.

sentences.trap: lam takes the PRESENT-shaped verb and makes it past: lam afham is I did not understand, never I do not understand. That pairing is L3-M4's and it is easy to unlearn after a level away from it.
sentences.sound: maʿ-NĀ carries the ʿayn before the n. af-HAM keeps the h light — it is the soft h, not the tight one of ḥārr.

variations.cue: What does this word mean?
variations.changed: the second half dropped — the question stands alone

variations.cue: I understood this word.
variations.changed: the report instead of the repair, in the plain past

mistake.display: āsif, lam afham. mā maʿnā hādhihi al-kalima
mistake.script: آسف، لم أفهم. ما معنى هذه الكلمة
mistake.why: Nothing here is wrong, but the apology is the English habit and it changes the register: opening every repair with āsif reads as distress. Ask the question first; the apology is for when you have actually cost someone something.

sentences.usage: Mid-conversation, when one word has stopped you. It keeps the exchange alive rather than ending it.
sentences.mnemonic: lam plus the present shape — and the meaning is past.

sentences.display: lam afham, hal yumkinuka an tuʿīd
sentences.script: لم أفهم، هل يمكنك أن تعيد
sentences.cue: I did not understand — could you repeat?
sentences.literal: not I-understood, question you-can that you-repeat

words.note: To do a thing again — say it again, here. uʿīd is I repeat, which is what you say when you are the one being asked.

sentences.trap: English softens this with a stack — could you possibly just repeat that. Arabic already has its softener in hal yumkinuka (L2-M1) and adding more only makes the sentence longer, not politer.
sentences.sound: tu-ʿĪD has the ʿayn between the vowels and a long ī. an tuʿīd runs together: an-tu-ʿīd.

variations.display: hal yumkinuka an tuʿīd hādhihi al-kalima
variations.script: هل يمكنك أن تعيد هذه الكلمة
variations.cue: Could you repeat this word?
variations.changed: what is to be repeated, named

variations.display: lam afham, hal yumkinuka an taqūl hādhā bi-ʿibāra ukhrā
variations.script: لم أفهم، هل يمكنك أن تقول هذا بعبارة أخرى
variations.cue: I did not understand — could you say this in other words?
variations.changed: the repair asked for: another wording rather than the same one again

mistake.why: yumkinuka needs an before its verb. English can you repeat has no that in it, and the missing particle is the single most common slip in the frame.

sentences.usage: Anywhere, to anyone. It is the sentence that buys you a second attempt without costing you any face.
sentences.mnemonic: yumkinuka AN — the particle is not optional.

sentences.display: hal yumkinuka an taqūl hādhā bi-ʿibāra ukhrā
sentences.script: هل يمكنك أن تقول هذا بعبارة أخرى
sentences.cue: Could you say this in other words?
sentences.literal: question you-can that you-say this in-phrase other

words.note: The restating frame, one unit. ukhrā is L4-M4's other, agreeing with the feminine ʿibāra — a phrase, a turn of words.

sentences.trap: English in other words usually introduces YOUR OWN restatement. Here it is being asked of someone else, and the difference is who does the work: this is a request, not a summary.
sentences.sound: bi-ʿi-BĀ-ra keeps the ʿayn right after the bi. UKH-rā opens on the kh and ends long.

variations.display: hādhā ṣaḥīḥ, bi-ʿibāra ukhrā huwa mumkin
variations.script: هذا صحيح، بعبارة أخرى هو ممكن
variations.cue: That is right — in other words, it is possible.
variations.changed: the speaker restating their own words, which is the frame's other use

variations.display: hal yumkinuka an tuʿīd bi-ʿibāra ukhrā
variations.script: هل يمكنك أن تعيد بعبارة أخرى
variations.cue: Could you repeat that in other words?
variations.changed: repeat rather than say — the two verbs share the frame

mistake.display: hal yumkinuka an taqūl hādhā bi-kalima ukhrā
mistake.script: هل يمكنك أن تقول هذا بكلمة أخرى
mistake.why: bi-kalima ukhrā asks for one different WORD, which is a much smaller request. The idiom is ʿibāra, a whole turn of phrase, and swapping the noun changes what you have asked for.

sentences.usage: When the words were clear and the meaning was not — a definition you followed and did not grasp.

sentences.cue: This is something like a chair.

words.note: The describing-around frame, and it is one key: L5-M5's shayʾ and L5-M1's mithl are both yours, but together they hedge, which neither does alone.
A chair, and here only an example of the frame — the point is the hedge in front of it, not the furniture.

sentences.trap: English hedges with or something at the END: a chair, or something. Arabic hedges at the FRONT and then names the thing plainly, so the softening arrives before the guess rather than after it.
sentences.sound: SHAYʾ ends on a hamza — a clean stop, not a vowel. al-KUR-sī holds the long ī at the end.

variations.cue: This is something like a dictionary.
variations.changed: what it is being compared to

variations.cue: It is something like tools.
variations.changed: the thing being described, and a plural on the far side of the frame

mistake.why: The frame cannot be stranded at the end. shayʾ mithl must come before the thing it likens to, and putting it last leaves a sentence that stops in the middle of a comparison.

sentences.usage: When you do not have the word and will not get it — the move that keeps you talking instead of stopping to look it up.

sentences.cue: It is a kind of tool.

words.cue: a kind of, a sort of
words.note: The other way around a gap: put the thing in a class instead of likening it to one. nawʿ alone is a kind, a type.
Tools of any trade, and it is already plural — there is no need to make it more plural.

sentences.trap: nawʿ min takes the DEFINITE plural after it — nawʿ min al-adawāt, a kind of the tools — where English takes a bare singular, a kind of tool. The article is not optional and the singular is not available.
sentences.sound: NAWʿ is one syllable with a diphthong, closing on the ʿayn. al-a-da-WĀT stresses the long ā near the end.

variations.cue: It is a kind of book.
variations.changed: the class it is put into

variations.cue: It is a kind of tool.
variations.changed: the subject — hiya for a feminine thing, and the frame does not move

mistake.why: A bare singular after min is the English shape. Arabic wants the definite plural of the class: nawʿ min al-adawāt. Getting this wrong is understood, but it marks the sentence as translated.

sentences.usage: Naming the category when the word itself is gone. It gets you further than shayʾ mithl when the thing has no close neighbour.
sentences.mnemonic: A kind of THE things — definite, and plural.

sentences.cue: How do you say this word in Arabic?

words.note: L1-M2's kayfa and L3-M5's taqūl, welded into the asking-for-a-word frame. Tapped as a pair it is this question; tapped apart it is only how and he says.

sentences.trap: English how do you say is a set phrase and so is this — but the Arabic uses the ordinary you-form of the verb, not an impersonal one. You are asking THIS person, and the sentence says so.
sentences.sound: KAY-fa ta-QŪL runs as four even beats with the long ū carrying the stress at the end.

variations.cue: How do you say this in Arabic?
variations.changed: pointing at a thing rather than naming a word

variations.cue: How do you say this phrase?
variations.changed: a whole phrase instead of a single word

mistake.why: yaqūl is he says. The frame is addressed to the person in front of you, so it must be taqūl — and the slip turns a question into a remark about somebody absent.

sentences.usage: Asking for a word you know the meaning of but not the sound of. The mirror of S01, which asks about the thing.
sentences.mnemonic: How do YOU say it — taqūl, never yaqūl.

sentences.cue: I do not know this word.

words.note: To know a THING or a person — a word, a street, a face. It is the verb the course ran thirty-nine modules without, and it is negated by lā, not by lam.

sentences.trap: English knows a word and knows that something is true with one verb. Arabic splits them: aʿrif for the word, aʿlam anna for the fact, and reaching for one where the other belongs is the level's most audible slip.
sentences.sound: aʿ-RIF squeezes the ʿayn immediately after the opening a — it is not a-rif. The final f is light.

variations.cue: I do not know this phrase.
variations.changed: what is unknown

variations.cue: You know this word.
variations.changed: the person, and the negation dropped

mistake.why: lam makes it past — I did not know it, at some earlier moment. The present state, not knowing it now, is lā aʿrif, and this is the pair L3-M4 opened.

sentences.usage: Said plainly and without apology. It is information the other person needs, not a confession.
sentences.mnemonic: aʿrif a thing; lā for now, lam for then.

sentences.display: aʿlam anna hādhā ṣaḥīḥ, lākin lā afham al-farq
sentences.script: أعلم أن هذا صحيح، لكن لا أفهم الفرق
sentences.cue: I know that this is right, but I do not understand the difference.
sentences.literal: I-know that this correct, but not I-understand the-difference

words.note: Knowing that something is SO, and L3-M3's anna follows it. Where aʿrif takes a thing, aʿlam takes a whole clause.
The difference between two things. It heads a possessive chain as readily as it takes bayna, between, after it; the r is tapped once, never rolled.

sentences.trap: An English speaker uses know for both halves of this sentence and then wonders why the Arabic has two verbs. The split is the rule: a clause after aʿlam, a noun after aʿrif, and no overlap.
sentences.sound: aʿ-LAM has the ʿayn straight after the a, like aʿrif. al-FARQ ends on a hard cluster: no vowel between the r and the q.

variations.cue: I know that this is right.
variations.changed: the second half dropped — aʿlam with its clause and nothing else

variations.cue: I do not understand the difference at all.
variations.changed: the second half standing alone, with L3-M3's tamāman on it

mistake.display: aʿrif anna hādhā ṣaḥīḥ, lākin lā afham al-farq
mistake.script: أعرف أن هذا صحيح، لكن لا أفهم الفرق
mistake.why: aʿrif wants a thing, not a clause. Once anna appears the verb must be aʿlam — this is the one place in the level where the English single verb costs you a wrong word rather than a wrong ending.

sentences.usage: The honest halfway repair: you followed the sentence and not the point, and saying which is which saves the other person guessing.

sentences.display: hādhā yusammā qāmūs aw kitāb tarjama
sentences.script: هذا يسمى قاموس أو كتاب ترجمة
sentences.cue: This is called a dictionary, or a translation book.
sentences.literal: this is-called dictionary or book translation

words.note: L4-M7's internal passive doing an ordinary job: the counter grammar and the table grammar are the same. tusammā for a feminine thing.
A dictionary, and one of the few classroom words worth saying out loud — the rest of that vocabulary is not what this module is for.
A REAL or: one thing or the other, and you must choose. It never means or something — that hedging is what shayʾ mithl and nawʿ min are for.
A translation, the noun. It heads a possessive chain here — kitāb tarjama, a book of translation — so neither word carries an article.

sentences.trap: English or something is a hedge and aw is not. hādhā qāmūs aw kitāb says you know it is exactly one of those two and are offering the pair — it does not say you are unsure what the thing is.
sentences.sound: yu-sam-MĀ doubles the m and ends on the long ā. AW is one syllable, a clean diphthong, never two beats.

variations.cue: This is called a translation.
variations.changed: the feminine of the passive, agreeing with hādhihi

variations.cue: This is called a chair.
variations.changed: what is being named — the frame answers S01's question

mistake.why: yusammā names a thing exactly; shayʾ mithl says you cannot. The two frames answer opposite situations, and stacking them says both at once.

sentences.usage: Giving the word back — the reply to somebody else's S01. It is the other half of every repair in this module.
sentences.mnemonic: aw offers a choice; mithl admits a gap.

comprehensionPool.script: لم أفهم، هل يمكنك أن تعيد
